newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Speech nothing to do with NZ leadership - Shipley.
newsitem.headline: Speech nothing to do with NZ leadership - Shipley.

text.p: State Services Minister Jenny Shipley said on Monday a speech given by her over the weekend was all to do with superannuation and not leadership.
News media speculated over the weekend that Shipley's speech to a National Council of Women seminar in Auckland was a precursor for an attempt on the National Party's leadership.
But Shipley, speaking on Radio New Zealand's Morning Report, said the speech dealt with how compulsory superannuation would damage the economy and be inequitable to women.
"This has absolutely everything to do with superannuation and nothing to do with leadership," Shipley said.

"The Treasurer has announced that an eight percent rate would buy an NZ$160,000 annuity. I simply made the point that, if that is the level for women, infact only 10 percent of New Zealand women will save $160,000 during their lifetime.

"The Treasurer has released those figures in a number of speeches. He would expect expect senior ministers, when invited to respond to large audiences, to give information so they can intelligently consider this matter and make a decision for themselves," she said.
Treasurer Winston Peters accused Shipley using the issue for political gain.
"I am asking my fellow politicians to address the issues of long term sustainability and not use their positions for short-term political gain," Peters said in a statement.
But Shipley said she had discussed the speech with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who backs the compulsory option, and Peters eight or 10 weeks ago.
"The PM argues that people like myself should be able to speak. He doesn't ask us not to. He encourages and defends the right of National MPs to put their point of view.
"I think it's quite inappropriate that such an important economic and social policy question should then be purported to be something other than what it is.

"My speech did not deal with personalities. It dealt in a substantive way with this issue. If the Treasurer doesn't like that, well quite frankly that is the public's right to make a judgement on the merits of personalities or substance.
"My personal agenda in relation to superannuation is to see that that women, people in the private sector, and those that are interested in politics understand the choices.

"There is a choice been voluntary and compulsion and I support voluntary and I intend to articulate those views clearly for the next six months so that New Zealanders can make a choice at the end of the year."
Shipley said Bolger had here support.

"The Prime Minister and I have worked together for seven years on all of the major social and economic policies. He has my total support in terms of the work we are doing at the moment. He has my total support as he defends the right of national MPs to debate this issue publically."
Shipley, ranked fifth in the Cabinet, is tipped as being the person most likely to succeed Bolger as party leader.
